Q1.answer: Whether normalizing each input window of a forecaster with the statistics of its own recent 48 steps (RWN) reduces forecast error when the series level shifts after training, compared with normalizing using fixed training statistics. The problem statement only becomes explicit in the Discussion; the Introduction opens with the experimental setup.

Q2.answer: Deployed forecasters (e.g. electricity demand) encounter level shifts, and most pipelines normalize with training statistics, which become stale after a shift. Both motivating assertions are uncited placeholders.
Q2.missing: Evidence or citations for the prevalence of level shifts and for standard normalization practice; both marked [CITATION NEEDED].

Q3.answer: According to the authors, existing evaluations change normalization and model capacity together, so the two explanations for shift-induced error (stale statistics vs. too-small model) are confounded. This rests on an unrun literature search.
Q3.missing: Any cited prior work; the gap claim is explicitly marked as not yet searched.

Q4.answer: Generated a synthetic hourly series (SynthLoad) with daily/weekly cycles and Gaussian noise; after a training year added level shifts of 0.2-0.8 training SDs; trained the same MLP (64 hidden units, 168h input, 24h horizon) under three normalizations: training-statistics baseline, RWN (per-window stats from last 48 steps), and RWN-fixed (stats estimated once from first 48 post-shift steps then frozen); 5 seeds each; reported mean and SD of test MAE.

Q5.answer: Holding the model identical across conditions is intended to isolate normalization from capacity. The window length 48 was chosen from a quick untuned trial. No rationale is given for the MLP, the synthetic generator, or the specific shift magnitudes.
Q5.missing: Rationale for the architecture, data generator, and window length (an author query is left in the text).

Q6.answer: Test MAE for baseline, RWN, and RWN-fixed on SynthLoad with no shift and shifts s in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}, 5 seeds per configuration. RWN-fixed appears to have been reported only at s = 0.6.
Q6.missing: Whether RWN-fixed was run at other shifts; test-period length; timing/shape of the shift; training budget details.

Q7.answer: No shift: RWN 0.409 +/- 0.007 vs baseline 0.412 +/- 0.006. At s = 0.6, RWN reduced MAE from 0.641 to 0.452 (~29%); across s = 0.2-0.6 reductions of 11-29%. RWN-fixed 0.518 at s = 0.6. At s = 0.8, RWN 0.712 +/- 0.021 vs 0.731 +/- 0.015 (no clear benefit).

Q8.answer: In this one synthetic setting with one fixed MLP, per-window normalization lowered MAE under moderate step level shifts without measurable cost when there is no shift, and a one-time re-estimation after the shift recovers roughly two thirds of the gain at s = 0.6.

Q9.answer: It does not show that stale statistics rather than capacity explain the error (capacity was never varied); it does not generalize to real data, other shift types, other architectures, or other window lengths; it does not establish a reliable 'boundary' at s = 0.8 from a one-SD gap with 5 seeds; the RWN-fixed ablation is a single shift magnitude with no reported spread and uses knowledge of when the shift occurred.

Q10.answer: A controlled synthetic comparison showing that rolling-window normalization reduces MAE by 11-29% under moderate level shifts without harming unshifted accuracy, plus an ablation suggesting most of the gain comes from a single re-estimation of statistics.

Q11.answer: Single synthetic generator; only level shifts; one fixed model capacity (not varied); untuned window length; 5 seeds; RWN-fixed only at one shift. The paper lists the first four.

Q12.answer: On a synthetic series, normalizing each input window with its own recent statistics cut forecast error by roughly 11-29% under moderate level shifts at no cost without shift, but not at the largest shift, and one re-estimate captured most of the gain.

inference_issues.missing_link: Capacity was never varied; holding it constant cannot show capacity is not a cause. Needs a capacity manipulation.

inference_issues.claim_text: Stale statistics rather than capacity may account for much of the error.
inference_issues.missing_link: Discussion admits capacity was not varied, yet the abstract keeps the capacity contrast without that bound or the synthetic-data bound.
Capacity was held constant, not controlled as an experimental factor; the label implies more than was done.

inference_issues.claim_text: an ablation attributing about a third of the gain to continued adaptation
inference_issues.missing_link: RWN-fixed reported at only s = 0.6, no seed spread; RWN-fixed also uses the known shift onset. General attribution needs the ablation across shifts with variability.

inference_issues.claim_text: a boundary at the largest shift
inference_issues.missing_link: Only one larger shift (0.8) with a ~1 SD gap over 5 seeds; this indicates no clear benefit, not an established boundary.

inference_issues.claim_text: across s = 0.2–0.6 the reduction was 11–29%, as Figure 1 shows
inference_issues.missing_link: Values for s = 0.2 and 0.4 and SDs at s = 0.6 are not reported; the figure has no displayed data.
0.409 +/- 0.007 vs 0.412 +/- 0.006 over 5 seeds supports no detected difference, not equivalence; no test or equivalence margin.

inference_issues.claim_text: Forecasters deployed on streams such as electricity demand meet level shifts
inference_issues.missing_link: Framing implies relevance to deployed load forecasting, but all evidence is from one synthetic generator with idealized step shifts.

objective_discrepancies: Objective asks how much gain depends on continued adaptation; the paper answers this at a single shift magnitude with no variability, yet the conclusion states it generally.
Objective does not mention model capacity, but the paper's abstract, discussion and conclusion frame the main takeaway as statistics-versus-capacity, which the design cannot test.

Objective says the reader should know what was tested; the paper conveys the setup but omits details (shift timing, output de-normalization, MAE units, test length) needed to understand exactly what was tested.
Objective emphasizes 'where the finding stops'; limitations are listed, but the abstract and conclusion do not carry them.
